title: Let’s talk about ‘masking’
author: Educating Hatbeasts
summary: A home-educating parent uses her younger son's experience in reception year to reframe the online argument over 'masking' in neurodivergent people. She argues the public debate is dominated by late-diagnosed adult women even though most diagnosed autistic people in the UK are children, many of whom can adapt well enough to hide their difficulties. Her view is that masking is ordinary social concealment, which everyone does, but intensified for children living with poorly understood hidden disabilities such as sensory overload, motor difficulties or uneven cognitive profiles. She describes her son hiding his academic ability, his handwriting struggles and his sensory discomfort at school to avoid standing out, and the change in him once he dropped that persona. She warns that obsessing over late diagnosis hands governments an excuse to strip support from children who plainly need it.
points: Because most diagnosed autistic people are under 18, a debate centered on late-diagnosed adults misses where most masking actually happens.
Masking can be understood as everyday fitting in at a larger scale, and in children it carries a real emotional cost because they learn to override their own discomfort.
Children with hidden, uneven profiles may conceal strengths as well as difficulties, so a child progressing at class pace may be performing, not limited.
Schools make adjustments for visible and global disabilities but rarely for varied, less visible differences that also shape learning.
Framing neurodiversity around the validity of late diagnosis risks giving authorities a political excuse to cut support for all children with developmental disabilities.
quotes: The problem with this is 60% of diagnosed autistic people in the UK are under 18 and 23% of those are aged under 10 (see table below). The vast majority of those under-18s diagnosed don’t have learning disabilities, which means they have the intelligence to adapt to their environment - to some extent, at least.
We all have a public persona. Most of us have multiple such personae, which we deploy in different situations. Most of us don’t want to stand out.
Living with poorly-understood hidden disabilities is exceptionally taxing in childhood. Children don’t get many choices in life.
The whole ‘masking’ conversation is, thus, not an autism-specific phenomenon (but I don’t think anyone intended it to be). It’s just everyday ‘fitting in’, but a lot more of it.

In children, this excessive concealment slowly does emotional damage as they’re hiding the wrong things, too much about themselves and they also get used to having their discomfort run roughshod over.
Their persona becomes, not about putting the best version of themselves forwards socially; it’s about pretending to be someone else entirely.
The reality is we lean over backwards, as we should, to help every young person to meet their potential - even if, far too often, we sadly don’t succeed.
